title: The night of awakening, in verse
hookLine: reread the Buddhacarita's canto of awakening (Buddhacarita 14)
tomorrow: a king won his war. what did he carve into stone?

cards: Every overnight success has a backstory: the band that came out of nowhere after years of empty bars. Buddhists have their own version of that argument, and it's about one night.
In Ashvaghosha's poem, the Buddhacarita, the Buddha sits down under a tree as the dark comes on, and by dawn he's awake. One night. Or was it?

teach.b: The Buddhacarita is a long poem of the Buddha's life, and its fourteenth canto is the night. He has just faced down Mara, and now he sits, still.
In the first watch, he remembers his past lives, one after another: names, families, joys and pains.

teach.h: SECOND: BEINGS BORN BY THEIR DEEDS.
teach.b: In the second, he sees all beings dying and being born again according to what they've done, and compassion rises in him.

teach.h: THIRD: HOW SUFFERING COMES TO BE.
teach.b: In the third, he looks into how suffering comes to be, link by link, back to ignorance. And at dawn, he knows. This is the night Buddhists celebrate at Vesak and on Bodhi Day.
Now the argument. One side says: look at the night. A human being sat down under a tree and woke before morning.

Awakening isn't a far-off prize for some other life; it can come in a single sitting, and some Chan and Zen teachers stressed exactly that, sudden awakening. The other side says: look at the first watch.
What does he spend it on? Remembering lives. The hare, and all the others.

teach.h: ONE SITTING, OR A LONG ROAD?
teach.b: The night is the last step of a very long road, and calling it instant hides the practice that made it possible. One side hears hope in the poem. The other hears honesty.
The poem keeps both: one night, and everything before it.

how: Buddhists celebrate the awakening at Vesak (with the Buddha's birth and passing) and, in Japan and some other communities, on Bodhi Day; some sit in meditation through the night to remember it.

games.q: what does “the night of awakening” mean?
o: the night under the tree when the Buddha fully woke
the night the Buddha left his palace in secret
a festival night of lanterns for the Buddha's birth

games.q: the night, watch by watch — tap the pairs.

s: the poem says the Buddha woke in a flash, with nothing before it
the first watch is spent remembering his past lives, one after another.
in the second watch he sees beings die and be reborn by their deeds
the Buddhacarita is part of the Pali canon
it's a Sanskrit poem by Ashvaghosha: one of the wider sources.

games.q: your study partner says the night proves awakening is sudden. you lean toward the long road. give her side's best case.
o: one human, one tree, one night: awakening can happen here, not only in some far-off life
she just wants a shortcut and doesn't like the idea of practice
she hasn't read the first watch, so her view doesn't count
games.why: the one-night side hears hope: it happened to a human being, in a single sitting. the long-road side answers with the first watch, full of past lives.

practice: Sit the way he sat: back upright, hands in your lap, one resting in the other. If it's evening, face a window and let the light go while you sit; if not, let the bell be your dusk.

wordCard.voice: The night of awakening: the Buddha's night under the tree, told in three watches, from remembering past lives to knowing at dawn.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Pali: awakening; what the night ends in.

carryVoice: Keep this one: the night of knowing, and every long night that led to it. Sit well.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 36 (the three knowledges in the night watches)
